reviewNotes: Full lesson text and five questions read. Scientific corrections, quantitative scope and quiz ambiguity reviewed against linked sources. This is a targeted educational review, not exhaustive certification. MCAT question-frequency claims are not independently verified.

replacements.old: The turn is stabilized by a **hydrogen bond between the carbonyl oxygen of residue *i* and the amide nitrogen of residue *i+3***—a single hydrogen bond spanning the turn.
replacements.new: Many beta turns have a **carbonyl O(i)···H–N(i+3) hydrogen bond**, but the usual geometric definition does not require this bond in every turn.

replacements.old: residue *i+2* can be any amino acid

replacements.old: Individual hydrogen bonds are weak (~2–5 kcal/mol in aqueous solution), but their cumulative effect across many residues provides substantial stability.
replacements.new: Their net contribution depends on geometry, solvent competition and conformational entropy; a single universal bond energy in water is not appropriate.

replacements.old: Secondary structure formation is favorable only when intramolecular backbone hydrogen bonds are more favorable than equivalent bonds with water—which is the case when the geometry is optimal and when the hydrophobic effect drives burial of nonpolar side chains.
replacements.new: Formation is favorable when the **total free-energy change** is negative, including protein interactions, solvent reorganization and loss of chain conformational entropy. Comparing individual hydrogen bonds with water is not sufficient.

replacements.old: While alpha helix stability is primarily driven by backbone hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic packing of interior residues also contributes significantly.
replacements.new: Backbone hydrogen bonds and side-chain packing both contribute to structure. Under the stated assumptions, burying an uncompensated charge is unfavorable.

replacements.old: Antiparallel beta sheets have evenly spaced, perpendicular hydrogen bonds and are generally more stable than parallel sheets
replacements.new: Antiparallel strands run in opposite directions and usually have straighter hydrogen bonds than parallel strands
replacements.reason: Test geometry rather than universal stability.

replacements.old: In antiparallel beta sheets, hydrogen bonds are evenly spaced and approximately perpendicular to the strand direction, creating a more linear and energetically favorable geometry that confers greater stability. Parallel beta sheets have hydrogen bonds that are more oblique and unevenly spaced, making them slightly less stable and requiring longer connecting loops. Choice C is partially true in that antiparallel sheets can be connected by beta turns, but parallel sheets also require connecting loops, so this does not correctly distinguish them.
replacements.new: Antiparallel strands have opposite N-to-C directions and relatively straight interstrand hydrogen bonds. Parallel strands run in the same direction and have more oblique hydrogen bonds. Neither geometry alone establishes whole-protein stability. Antiparallel strands need not be joined by a short beta turn; they may be connected by longer loops or belong to different chains.

replacements.old: Glycine, because it lacks a side chain and can adopt phi/psi angles in regions of the Ramachandran plot forbidden to other amino acids
replacements.new: Glycine, because its hydrogen R group permits positive phi angles with fewer steric constraints

replacements.old: Glycine is unique in lacking a side chain (its R-group is simply a hydrogen), allowing it to adopt phi and psi angles in regions of the Ramachandran plot that are sterically inaccessible to all other amino acids.
replacements.new: Glycine has a hydrogen R group, so positive phi angles are less sterically restricted than for most other residues.
replacements.reason: Other residues can occur at positive phi.
